pedagogy.summary:
- **Age:** 11–12 years

- **Topic:** The Particle Model

- **Standards — UK (DfE KS3 Physics 'Matter' — Particle model & Physical changes):** The differences in arrangements, in motion and in closeness of particles explaining changes of state, shape and density, the anomaly of ice-water transition; atoms and molecules as particles; density differences between solids, liquids and gases. (DfE KS3 Chemistry: properties of states in terms of the particle model, including gas pressure.)

- **Standards — US (NGSS MS-PS1-4):** [curriculum wording omitted; reference MS-PS1-4] (qualitative molecular-level models).

- **Operational details:** This is the FULL KS3 particle model: using arrangement, spacing and motion to EXPLAIN properties, not just depict them. Targets: (1) compressibility — only gases compress because only they have large empty gaps; (2) density — gases are far less dense because the same particles are spread through much more space; (3) the ice-water anomaly — water is unusual because its solid (ice) is LESS dense than its liquid (particles lock into an open, spaced structure on freezing), which is why ice floats. Also gas pressure as particle collisions with container walls. Build each explanation from a particle diagram/sim and reason from it. This node assumes fluent particle diagrams (prereq) and extends the introductory model. Keep qualitative; formal kinetic theory and gas laws are later.

- **Checkpoint:** Tier B–C (early-formal). The child uses particle arrangement/spacing/motion to explain compressibility AND relative density across states, and explains why ice floats via the open structure of solid water — without treating individual particles as changing size or property.
bestPractices: Derive each property (compressibility, density, floating ice) FROM particle arrangement/spacing, rather than stating it alongside a diagram.
Contrast the three states on the same screen so density and compressibility differences are read from spacing.
Treat the ice-water anomaly as a deliberate 'exception that proves the model' — the open lattice explains why ice floats.
Introduce gas pressure as particle collisions with the walls, keeping it qualitative.
Reinforce that particles keep their size and identity; only spacing, pattern and motion change.
keyRepresentations: A three-state particle sim with a compression piston
A per-box particle counter as a density meter
A water-freeze mode showing the open, spaced ice lattice growing in volume
A wall-collision counter representing gas pressure
commonMisconceptions: Solids are denser because their particles are 'bigger/heavier', not because they are closer packed.
All solids are denser than their liquids (missing the water/ice anomaly).
Gas pressure comes from particles pushing on each other rather than colliding with the walls.
Particles expand or change on heating rather than moving faster and spreading.

learn.summary: Learners aged 11–12 use the particle model (arrangement, spacing and motion) to EXPLAIN — not just depict — compressibility, relative density, and the ice-water anomaly, keeping particle size and identity fixed. The core activity derives each property from a manipulable particle model: compress each state, count particles per box (a qualitative count-based density proxy for one substance across states) to compare density, and freeze water to watch it lock into an open, spaced lattice that takes up more room (so ice floats). Alternatives include a reveal-panel summary companion, a matching/sequencing check, a predict-observe-explain syringe task, and an optional 3D ice-lattice view. Gas pressure is introduced qualitatively as particle collisions with container walls. Formal kinetic theory and gas laws are deliberately left for later. The density ordering solid > liquid > gas is the typical pattern, with water deliberately treated as the exception (ice less dense than liquid water).

activities.title: Particle explainer: derive compressibility, density and floating ice from a model
feedback: If a learner says the gas particles get squashed smaller: in this model the particles keep the same size — what changes is the space between them. Redraw before/after with same-size dots and smaller gaps.

If a learner says gases are less dense because their particles are smaller or lighter: the particles are the same; a gas simply spreads the same particles through much more space, so fewer sit in each box.

If a learner predicts ice sinks or says it is denser because it is solid: water is the anomaly — its particles lock into a MORE open arrangement when frozen, so ice is LESS dense and floats; contrast with the usual solid-denser pattern.

If a learner attributes expansion on heating to particles growing: particles don't grow — for most substances they move faster and spread further apart, so the substance takes up more room while each particle stays the same size (liquid water between 0 °C and about 4 °C is an exception: it contracts when heated); anchor to 'same particles, more space'.
If a learner treats the per-box count as the actual density: clarify it is a qualitative proxy showing more particles in the same space means denser, not a literal measurement.
activities.rationale: Explaining density, compressibility and the ice anomaly each involve manipulating particle spacing and reading off the consequence, so a model the learner can compress, count and freeze is proposed to turn each abstract explanation into an observed cause-and-effect. Research cited for this topic (marked unverified in the source row) reports that students struggle to explain density/compressibility via spacing and often think particles themselves change, with the ice-water anomaly a key explanatory target. The NGSS claim is relevant to the freeze/state-change step rather than to the compression and density derivations.
sourceClaims: DfE KS3 Physics 'Matter/Particle model': arrangement/motion/closeness of particles explain changes of state, shape and density, the anomaly of ice-water transition; atoms and molecules as particles; density differences between states
NGSS MS-PS1-4: develop a qualitative molecular-level model predicting/describing changes in particle motion, temperature and state
Students struggle to explain density/compressibility via spacing and often think particles themselves change; the ice-water anomaly is a key explanatory target
learnerActions: Squeeze a piston on a solid, then a liquid, then a gas in a particle simulation; observe that only the gas yields noticeably while a callout shows its empty gaps closing and the close-packed states barely move.
State in your own words why only gases compress much — because only they have large empty spaces between particles to remove, not because particles shrink.

Use a per-box particle counter to compare how many particles fill the same box in each state of the same substance; read off that a gas has far fewer particles in the same space, so it is far less dense. Treat this count as a qualitative, count-based proxy for density (valid for one substance across states), not a literal mass/volume measurement.
Cool liquid water and watch the particles snap into an OPEN, spaced lattice that visibly takes up MORE room; see the resulting ice float on liquid water.
Explain why water is the odd one out — its solid is LESS dense than its liquid because particles lock into an open, spaced structure on freezing — and connect this to why ponds freeze top-down.
Switch to a gas-pressure mode that counts particle hits on the container walls, and describe gas pressure as the result of those collisions with the walls.
activities.intendedInsight: The same model — particles of fixed size whose spacing, pattern and motion change — explains compressibility, relative density across states, and the anomalous floating of ice. The explanation is read off the arrangement, not asserted alongside a picture.

activities.title: Predict–Observe–Explain: syringe of air vs syringe of water
feedback: Full understanding: uses particle spacing to explain compressibility, low gas density, AND ice floating, keeping particles fixed in size throughout — the model transfers across all three phenomena.

Partial: explains compressibility by inter-particle space for the gas/liquid case but can't yet extend spacing to density or the anomalous expansion of water — one application, not the model; re-run the density and freeze challenges.

Gap: explains compression by shrinking particles or gas 'disappearing' and can't link density or floating ice to arrangement; redraw same-size dots with changing gaps and reconnect to the particle diagram.
For oil: like water, a liquid is close-packed with little inter-particle space, so it barely compresses — the reason rests on spacing, not on the specific substance.
activities.rationale: Probing the mechanism rather than the fact is intended to discriminate understanding, because the same inter-particle-space idea underlies compressibility, density and anomalous expansion. A hands-on syringe prediction makes the learner commit to a causal account before seeing the result. The DfE claim supports the represented properties rather than independently validating the discrimination point.
sourceClaims: DfE KS3 Physics 'Matter/Particle model': arrangement/motion/closeness of particles explain changes of state, shape and density, the anomaly of ice-water transition; atoms and molecules as particles; density differences between states
learnerActions: Before pushing, predict which sealed plunger will push in and how far: a syringe of air (plunger out) or a syringe of water (plunger out), and say WHY in terms of particles.
Push both plungers: observe that air compresses markedly while water barely moves.

Explain the result: in a gas the particles are far apart with empty space between them, so pushing brings them closer (you compress the SPACE, not the particles); in a liquid the particles are already touching (close-packed but disordered), so there is almost no space to remove.

Answer follow-ups: When you squash the air, what gets smaller — the particles or the gaps? Draw it. Using particles, why is a gas much less dense than a solid? What must be different about how particles are arranged in ice so it floats? If it had been oil instead of water, compressible or not, and why the same as water?
activities.intendedInsight: The pre-observation reasoning about space between particles — not the observation itself — is intended to be the diagnostic that separates understanding spacing from thinking particles get squashed or the gas 'disappears'.

activities.title: Spacing-explains-property reveal panel (consolidation companion)
feedback: If a learner reads the flap text without linking it to the picture, ask them to point to the exact spacing difference that causes the property.
For the ice panel, prompt: which arrangement has particles spread into more space — the liquid or the solid — and how does that set the density?
activities.rationale: A static reveal panel is a useful summary and reference after manipulation; because it cannot be compressed, frozen or measured, it consolidates rather than derives the explanations, so it works best paired with the simulation.
learnerActions: Study a contrasting panel showing particle spacing for solid, liquid and gas side by side.
Reveal the 'why it compresses / why it's less dense / why ice floats' flaps and restate each explanation in your own words, pointing to the spacing that causes it.
Open the key panel contrasting ordinary liquid water with its open ice lattice and explain why the open structure makes ice less dense.
activities.intendedInsight: Having the three states and their explanations visible together is intended to consolidate that one spacing-based model accounts for all three properties.

activities.title: Match and order: properties to particle explanations
feedback: If typical density ordering is wrong, return to the per-box counter: more particles in the same space means denser.
If a learner extends solid > liquid > gas to claim ice must sink, re-surface the anomaly: ice floats because its solid arrangement is more open, not because solids are always denser.
If a learner matches 'floats' to 'is solid', re-surface the anomaly: ice floats because its solid arrangement is more open, not simply because it is solid.
activities.rationale: Matching and sequencing are apt checks when the target is explanation-from-model, but as recognition formats they do not by themselves require the learner to construct an explanation, so they belong after the derivation work; the density-ordering step is scoped to the typical pattern so it does not contradict the water anomaly.
learnerActions: Match each property (compressible, dense, floats) to the particle-arrangement explanation that causes it.
Order the three states by density for a typical substance (solid > liquid > gas) and justify the order from particle spacing.
Then flag water as the deliberate exception: explain why ice (solid water) is LESS dense than liquid water, so it does not fit the usual solid-denser pattern.
Work through this after the simulation so the matching tests explanation-from-model, not recall of labels.
activities.intendedInsight: Pairing a property with its spacing-based cause, ranking the typical states by density, and recognising water as the exception checks that the learner reasons from the model rather than reciting a blanket rule.

activities.title: Optional 3D view of the open ice lattice
feedback: If the 3D view distracts from the spacing point, return to the 2D diagram, which conveys the anomaly adequately.
activities.rationale: The curriculum works from 2D particle diagrams and a 2D simulation conveys spacing and the anomaly adequately, so a 3D view is an optional cameo offered when the open structure is hard to read in 2D — a different spatial experience, not a required one.
learnerActions: If the open structure is hard to read in 2D, rotate a 3D packing view of the ice lattice to see how particles sit in a more open, spaced arrangement than in liquid water.
Compare the 3D open lattice with the close-packed arrangement and connect the extra space to lower density.
activities.intendedInsight: Density and the ice lattice are genuinely spatial, so seeing the open structure in three dimensions may make the 'more open means less dense' link clearer for some learners.

constraints: Keep everything qualitative: formal kinetic theory and gas laws are for later study.
Reinforce throughout that particles keep their size and identity; only spacing, pattern and motion change — never depict particles shrinking, growing, or 'disappearing'.
This node assumes learners are already fluent with particle diagrams; it extends the introductory model to explanation.
Treat the ice-water case as the deliberate anomaly: the typical pattern is solid denser than liquid, but do not let learners generalise 'all solids are denser than their liquids'.
Introduce gas pressure only as particle collisions with the container walls, not as particles pushing on each other.

Reveal panels, matching and sequencing are recognition/consolidation formats: they do not by themselves require the learner to construct an explanation, so use them after the derivation activity, not instead of it.

A flat screen simulation or diagram represents three-dimensional particle arrangements; name it as a model of the real spatial packing rather than the packing itself, and treat per-box particle counts as a qualitative count-based density proxy (valid for one substance across states), not a literal density measurement.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The source claim that students struggle to explain density/compressibility via spacing and that the ice-water anomaly is a key target is marked unverified (verified:false) in the row; treat it as motivation, not established efficacy.
The simulation's hexagonal-style ice lattice and volume increase are design choices to make the anomaly visible; present them as a model of real ice structure, not a measured demonstration.

Claims that a dialogue 'cannot' generate spacing evidence or that only the simulation teaches these ideas have been softened: the manipulable model is proposed for its affordance (manipulate-and-read-off), not asserted as uniquely necessary.
Density ordering is scoped to the typical solid>liquid>gas pattern with water flagged as the exception, to avoid reinforcing the 'solids always denser' misconception the node targets.
The NGSS claim retained on activity[0] directly supports the freeze/state-change step; its application to the compression and density derivations is only topical.

assess.poeTask: Predict-Observe-Explain: seal a syringe of air and a syringe of water, both plungers out. Ask the child to predict which plunger will push in, how far, and WHY. A child who thinks particles get squashed predicts both compress. Push both: air compresses markedly, water almost none. The pre-observation reasoning about space between particles is the diagnostic part.
probeDeeper: When you squash the air, what exactly gets smaller — the particles or the gaps? Draw it.
A gas is much less dense than a solid. Using the particles, why?
Ice floats on water. What must be different about how the particles are arranged in ice?
If it had been a syringe of oil instead of water — compressible or not? Why the same as water?
assess.correctAnswer: In a gas the particles are far apart with empty space between them, so pushing brings them closer — you're compressing the SPACE, not the particles. In a liquid the particles are already touching (close-packed, just disordered), so there's almost no space to remove — hence it barely compresses. The reason rests on SPACING between particles, and on the particles themselves not shrinking.

errorPatterns.pattern: the particles themselves get squashed/smaller when you compress a gas
errorPatterns.nextMove: Particles are incompressible — what changes is the space between them. Redraw before/after: same-size dots, smaller gaps. Reconnect to the particle diagram.
errorPatterns.distractor: The air particles get squashed smaller when you push the plunger.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: explains compression as shrinking particles rather than closing the gaps between them

errorPatterns.pattern: heating makes each particle expand, which is why things expand when heated
errorPatterns.nextMove: Particles don't grow — they move faster and take up more room, so spacing increases. Anchor to 'same particles, more space'.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: attributes thermal expansion to particles growing rather than moving more and spacing out

errorPatterns.pattern: ice sinks / ice is denser because it's solid ('solids are always denser than their liquid')
errorPatterns.nextMove: Water is the anomaly: its particles lock into a MORE open arrangement when frozen, so ice is LESS dense and floats. Contrast with the usual solid-denser pattern.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: predicts ice sinks, or can't explain why it floats using particle arrangement

responseLevels.gap: Explains compression by shrinking particles or gas 'disappearing'; can't link density or floating ice to arrangement.
responseLevels.full: Uses particle spacing to explain compressibility, low gas density, AND ice floating (more open arrangement in solid water), keeping particles fixed in size throughout — the model transfers across all three phenomena.
responseLevels.partial: Explains compressibility by inter-particle space for the gas/liquid case, but can't yet extend the spacing idea to density or the anomalous expansion of water — one application, not the model.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: You can squash a sealed syringe full of air to half its size, but a sealed syringe full of water barely moves at all. Using what you know about particles, why can you compress the gas but not the liquid? Give me the picture in your head, then the reason.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: The tier-two reason separates a child who explains compressibility by inter-particle SPACE from one who thinks the particles themselves are being squashed or that the gas 'disappears'. The same error surfaces with density and anomalous expansion — so probing the mechanism, not the fact, is what discriminates.
